Their timing in the play concepts, those are something we're always working on and I think they're doing a good job with that. Skill guys are grinding through things. So, it's been a It's been a good start. We got two two more days here to to go. But all this leads up to training camp. So, this OTA practice, if you will, is for learning. It's for making mistakes. It's for doing some different things. And then you come back and you tighten it up for training camp. As they'll find out, the the train is going to be moving pretty quickly come in July. So, this is a really a an introduction phase, a learning phase, and a correction phase. >> With Cam, how do you balance that understanding hey, it's just OTAs, but also understanding the importance of some of the inaccuracy issues that that he's had being corrected? >> Now, he's had some very good accurate plays, too. Again, this is this is the initial part of the offense, if you will. So, you take it from the classroom, which was in April, and then you lead on to May and June to this. I don't think we ever say it's just OTAs or it's just practice. You want to try to be elite every time you step out on the field. But coaching the quarterbacks for a long time, there's a lot of things that go go into quarterback play. Even just getting familiarity with with some of the skill players around you. But I'm very pleased with where he's at. Understands the offense well. I think his feet are really good. His eye discipline, his vision down the field. And I've been pleased with with his progress. >> Talked a lot about a lot of the misses. >> I'm sorry, who did you say first? >> Robert. >> Okay. many of Cam's misses being related to to the newness. But like Tuesday, there were two balls in relative short order that he was throwing to Alec on the left side and he hit Calligan in the back on both of them. Which seemed to a layman like that's a standard quarterback ball where he's just got to get enough loft of it over the DB. Is that in any way system related or is that a quarterback being inaccurate? >> Well, I think you have to look at the whole picture and see where the deep safeties are and the tempo and arc and pace that you need to throw with the football. Controlling the middle of field safety, using your eyes the right way, movement. There's different adjustments that receivers have relative to when the ball is coming, how quickly it's coming. Is it an over top throw? Is it a back shoulder throw? All those things are tied in together, Paul. It's not the quarterback, it's not the receiver, it's a line. It's everybody that terms of completing a successful play. But he's he's had plenty of those good ones, too. So, again, what what I'm looking for is our grasp, being able to operate quickly, having our eyes in the right spot, being able to move defenders when we need to move them, slight reset and throws when we need to have them, and give our guys a chance. And I think each each practice we go back in there, we look at the tape, have a lot of confidence in in Cam. I have a lot of confidence in the other quarterbacks as well. >> How much of it is How much of it, Brian, is apples to apples when we see Cam have a day that, you know, where we see him and maybe he hits 50% of the throws versus Mitch hitting 70 or Will hitting 65 or 70? How much is apples to apples in what we're seeing out here? >> Well, we don't really repeat plays. So, every play is a unique play in and of itself. I might give you a quick throw. I might give him an intermediate throw. I might give you a deep throw. There might be no outlets. There might be a pressure where your outlet has to stay in. Every play is unique in and of And you know, the quarterback's job is to go out there and try to make the right decision. His decisions have been excellent. And then, you know, complete a pass. But there's, you know, completions, you know, I've coached receivers, I've coached tight ends, I've coached quarterbacks, backs. Um, you know, everybody's got to be on the same page with that. And we're working We're working on that. That's what this time of year is for. >> Everybody Everybody needs time away. But what what expectations for Cam and everybody else maybe on offense, what you leave here at the end of this week? >> Um, well, my focus is on these next 2 days. So, you know, those guys have a will have a good plan once they leave here. They always do. I'm quite sure that the quarterbacks and a bunch of the skill guys will throw at some point. Um, but they're going to have to, you know, stay in the playbook the best they can, make sure they're in elite physical condition, work on some of the things that, you know, the coaches are going to ask them to work on, and come back ready to go, healthy, in shape, and be ready for a tough training camp. >> Brian, with Cam but behind the scenes, what are maybe some of the ways you're trying to push him, like in ways that we're not seeing as laymen in in How is he responded to the way you're you're trying to push him? >> Uh, push him and what coach him and teach him is what we're trying to do. Again, he's uh He's got very good awareness, field vision, instincts. And you go out there, you practice, you do individual drills, you go to seven-on-seven or team settings. You know, we've done a a good amount of situational work. And you come in and you correct it or you praise it. Uh but you you teach it. That's what we're At the end of the day, we're teachers. We got to do a good job of teaching. And uh he's a good student to teach. >> When we talk about accuracy, in your experience, is that something that can be taught or improved throughout a career or is that something that's one of those more innate traits that somebody just kind of has? >> Uh well, I mean, a lot of people talk about accuracy. That's the job of a quarterback. Um You know, I've had guys that have had high completion percentages that had low completion percentages the year prior. Um you know, Cam can make all the throws. He's going to be a good quarterback. >> Where are you guys with uh option routes and how much of an adjustment is that to to to Cam and to a lot of his targets? Where's the progress on that? How do you feel guys are in sync? >> What kind of option routes are you talking about? >> I I don't know. Maybe you could tell me. >> Uh well, I just want to I'm trying to give you the answer you're looking for. Uh so, there's a lot of option routes in our offense. Uh there's slot option routes. There's outside vertical option routes. There's inside intermediate option routes. Uh sometimes the receiver has a three-way go on a route that that we throw one direction and the receiver goes the other direction. And sometimes um you know, the receiver sees one thing in his route and the quarterback's waiting on it and sees a different thing. So, you throw the ball away, you move on to the next play. But you know, those can take considerable amount of time. Um they're all different. So, they have uh you know, they have to start with what the coverage is. Uh the receiver and the quarterback. Where is the defensive help? Where is the leverage of the defender? What can I do? What can I do as a as a receiver? But we've we've had plenty of them and you you're always working on those. I think this is a good time of year to work on these. Ball to figure out, you know, who you can really trust, the body language of one player in particular the other. They all run a little bit different. Some are taller linear guys. Some are shorter quicker guys. And you can do them on air and practice on air, but there's there's nothing like the the game rep or the practice rep against the defense that gives you the different looks that you're going to see as a quarterback and in particular as a receiver. I'd say that the inside breaking option routes, if you will, are maybe a little bit more difficult than the outside just because there's extra defenders in the box and both the quarterback and the skill player, whoever that may be. We do it with backs. We do it tight ends. We do it receivers. That requires a lot of work. And there's mistakes, you know, you see it one way, the receiver sees it the other way and then you go back and you sit down and usually those meetings that we have when we're talking about those those those go a little bit longer cuz I want to make sure that they're all communicating to what they're saying and then most importantly what the quarterback's saying, but when you have an option route, a lot of times that's on the skill player to make the correct decision and the quarterback's waiting on it. So you might be a tad bit late, but you want to be right on that. >> With your ascension to those slot routes, the choice routes, and things like that with Wan'Dale and your past experience, that process of getting on the same page, was that a lengthy process and how do you think that's going to be here with he and Cam developing that? >> Yeah, I think we're making we're making good progress with it, but again, you have to do it and you have to make the mistakes and you have to see it. title: Questions surround Sorsby in supplemental draft + Rashee Rice released | PFTPM (FULL) | NFL on NBC
text: It's PFT live hiatus time, which means it's PFT PM time, which means it's Tuesday, June 16. It's time to get down to business. The supplemental draft had been irrelevant for seven years. They had one in 2023, no one was picked. The last time someone was selected, 2019. There have been multiple recognizable names over the years who have entered the NFL through the supplemental draft. It has become something that is used less and less frequently in these days, but it will be a major topic in the coming days and weeks as Brendan Sorsby decides to abandon his attempt to play college football and applies for the supplemental draft. And there are a lot of questions and I've talked about some of this stuff before, but I think this is a good moment to really frame up the three big questions going forward from this point. Number one, will the NFL accept Brandon Sorsby, Brandon Sorsby, excuse me, into the supplemental draft? There's no reason for them not to. He's no longer eligible to play college football. He was eligible to play college football back in April when the regular draft happened. And the way the CBA is written, if a player becomes ineligible after the the regular draft, he can enter the supplemental draft. And he meets all the other criteria. He's at least three years out of high school. That's the one big one. So, there's nothing that should keep him out. That doesn't mean the NFL won't try to find a way to do it. The NFL's been tight lipped about this one, so we don't know what they are thinking. The way the CBA is written, you could make the argument if you want to try to keep Brendan Sorsby out that he knew or should have known he was ineligible in advance of the most recent regular draft and he should have entered that draft. He could have. He's got the time in. He could have declared for it. He had reason to know he may not be able to play in 2026 because he's aware of his gambling habits. his gambling activities, his violation of gambling laws because he was gambling when he was under the age of 21 and his violation rampant and repeated violation of NCA bylaws. Now, that would be a very aggressive argument for the NFL to make, but that would be based on my reading of the CBA the only thing they could do if they really want to just kick this can until April of next year. They could do that. They could say you knew or at a minimum should have known you had lost your eligibility. It just wasn't official yet. You should have entered the regular draft in April and you decided to try to get two bites out of the apple. You decided to try to keep your eligibility, fight the NCA, and then when the walls closed in legally, you changed your mind and you bolted for the NFL. That's not me talking. That's what the NFL would say if they were to make that argument that he knew or should have known he was eligible for the regular draft. And therefore, he can't choose his draft. He can't pick which draft he gets selected in. Can't try to have it both ways trying to stay in college and then if all else fails, I'll go to the NFL draft. And clearly once this thing became an issue, he was trying to get clarity from the NCAA so he could make that decision. Are you going to let me play? I want to play at Texas Tech. Are you going to let me play? No. All right. I got an injunction that says you have to let me play. Problem solved. Then other lawsuits get filed. The heat got a little too hot for Texas Tech and Sorsby, I think, sensitive to what Texas Tech has been going through. He pulls the plug and he has the supplemental draft. I think they should let him in. But if they want to be ultraaggressive, they could make that argument that he'd already lost his eligibility and he knew it. and it became a shell game after that for him to try to get one more year of college football, one more year of NIL money before coming to the NFL. Second question, will he be suspended by the NFL? You let him into the supplemental draft and then you impose a suspension for violation of the law underage betting and rampid violations of the NCA gambling rules. That one's a little trickier. I've mentioned the Terrell Prior president several times. He had a five-game suspension imposed on him for the 2011 season. He ended up entering the supplemental draft. The NFL imposed the same fivegame suspension, arguing that he manipulated the eligibility rules in a way that undermines the integrity of them. It wouldn't be very difficult for the NFL to come up with something, if it wants to, to make the case that betting while under the age of 21 repeatedly, betting on your team, even if you weren't playing in games, that that requires the same punishment he's escaping by leaving the NCAA. Now, it's not a perfect argument, and most legal arguments aren't. That's why there's two sides to every story. One side tries to fashion an argument rooted in relevant applicable rules language that suits their interest. The other side goes the other way. Good lawyers can come up with compelling arguments on both sides of a question. But if the NFL really wants to be not full out aggressive and keep him out of the supplemental draft, welcome him in, but suspend him. What's to stop them? He's not protected by the union until he's drafted or signs an NFL contract. So, they could, and this where this is where the the timing of a suspension becomes interesting. You suspend him before he's drafted. What standing would the union have at that point to do anything? None. Once he's drafted, the union has the ability to fight it. I don't know that the NFL will try to split the hairs that carefully. They may just wait and see if he's drafted. Now, I think he will be. More on that in a second, but it could be the NFL doesn't do anything about a possible suspension until it has to, and it doesn't have to until after he's drafted. So, the Terrell Prior case from 2011 could make a suspension more likely for Sorsby. And I know that there are teams that are concerned they're going to draft this guy and he's not going to be available at all in 2026. So what's the point in giving up the draft pick early if you don't get the benefit of the player early? Another item that I believe I've mentioned here and I wrote something about it today at PFT. Kahan Booty, very similar case, gambling addiction, admitted to it, wrote an article for the Players Trabune earlier this year between conference championships, I believe in the Super Bowl. He was drafted by the Patriots in 2023. After his rookie season, it came to light that he was being arrested for underage gambling in Louisiana, made at least six bets on LSU while he was on the LSU team. The charges were later dropped and the NFL did nothing. Nothing. Now, the big difference is he was already in the NFL for a season. And from a PR standpoint, and so much of this stuff really is PR, the decisions the NFL makes from a disciplinary standpoint, the personal conduct policy in and of itself is a PR tool. It's not a judicial tool. It's a quasi judicial device to enhance and promote and support the NFL's PR efforts. But if you act against Booty after he's been in the NFL for a full season, you draw attention to the fact that you had no idea. What kind of vetting are you guys doing when you have no idea that this guy who you have welcomed into the draft class was rampantly and repeatedly gambling? So, I could see why the NFL decides not to do anything with Booty because he's already in the NFL. But with Sorsby, it's front and center. It's a big deal. In the aftermath of last week's court ruling, it was one of the biggest stories in sports. So even though what they didn't do with Kahan Booty would seem to apply and would seem to suggest they shouldn't do anything with Brenton Sorsby, the difference is they know about Sorsby before he ever plays. And we we know we know how the NFL operates. This isn't criticism. It's reality. They do whatever they want to do case by case. They don't like to be bound by precedent. They don't like to have third parties making decisions based on past practices and fairness, etc. They just want to do what they think is right in this case. What is right for us right now? Right now, this is a big deal. A lot of questions about integrity of sport and big headlines and a lot of discussion and let's just take some of the steam out of this. And also, as I've said before, they may want to plate the NCAA. If the NCA doesn't want this guy to play in 2026, if they view it as a punishment, he shouldn't be allowed to play in 2026, if that's conveyed directly or indirectly, overtly or subtly to the NFL, they may feel compelled to to act accordingly. The last bit of precedent, and this is from a question that a reader asked, I had forgotten about this. When Jim Harbaugh left Michigan for his return to the NFL, at one point Ian Raport of NFL media, which at the time was owned and operated by the league, said basically if Harbaugh comes back, he's going to get suspended because he's subject to suspension by the NCAA. Well, that never happened. There was never anything. It was never even a serious conversation publicly about the possibility of Harbaugh suffering any consequences for the various things that went on when he was at Michigan. So if I'm arguing on behalf of Brendan Sorsby, I'm pointing to Harbaugh and I'm pointing to Kahan Booty and I'm pointing out that what they did to Terrell Prior in 15 years ago shouldn't have happened. And as we reported last night, Jeffrey Kesler already putting the NFL on notice. I'm told that he's going to make sure that they don't try to either not accept him into the supplemental draft or suspend him once he gets there. Now, the bigger question is this, and this relates to what happens if he's allowed into the supplemental draft, and it's time for the teams to start figuring out what they're going to do. And the procedure, I found this in an SI article from about the time this all first came up. They split the league into three categories. Teams with six or fewer wins or fewer than six wins. Teams with six or more wins that didn't make the playoffs and then all the teams that made the playoffs. So, you have three buckets of teams. They do a weighted lottery. So, there really is an NFL draft lottery. We just didn't we didn't really know about it. They haven't monetized it yet. It's not a tent pole event yet. The supplemental draft lottery, but they do a lottery to determine who's got priority among those three buckets. And then each round the team decides ahead of time, am I basically going to bid? It's like a silent auction. I'm going to bid this pick and you bid it for let's say round three, well, if you have priority as opposed to the other teams that made the bid, you get him. That's a dynamic that could get someone who maybe made the playoffs last year or got close to it think better go around earlier if I want this guy. So if the consensus is he's round three, you may have to go round two to get him. if you're going to be low in the priority list, but everybody will know what their priority is. So, that's part of the the guessing game that a team is going to need to make. Do I pull the trigger this round or do I wait until next round because next round somebody higher in the pecking order may get him before we can. the separate question and this is again crystallized by all of the criticism, all the discussion, the hand ringing, everything that happened after the ruling was issued last Monday. Will there be teams that shy away from Brendan Sorsby? You got 32 teams now. 31 can say no. All it takes is one to say yes. I don't think it's ludicrous to think there are some teams and specifically their owners. When you're talking about significant draft capital, the owner is going to be involved. When you're talking about getting a quarterback who could be groomed to become your future starter, the owner is going to be involved. And if the owner isn't comfortable with what is known or knowable between now and the time the supplemental draft comes, if you're not comfortable, you're not going to greenlight it. Quarterback touches the ball every single play. We don't need to have on our team the risk of a quarterback who has a gambling addiction that he's trying to recover from having a relapse. We don't want to spend our time policing him hard enough to run a football team without having to constantly monitor one of the players who has a gambling addiction in a sport that is fueled by gambling where the owners are allowed to own up to 5% of a company that runs a sports book. where the NFL has traditionally, not yet, but they eventually will, had lucrative sponsorships with sports books, where you see the ads everywhere. We're not comfortable taking that chance. That's going to be the balance. And there will be some owners who are conservative, small C conservative, who are careful, and they just don't want to they don't want to run that risk. You got to weigh the talent against the risk. And that becomes part of this analysis as well. How good do we think he'll be based upon his time primarily at Cincinnati? Will he be potentially a consistent, viable starting quarterback? Could he become a Pro Bowler? Could he become a franchise quarterback? And you know, there are teams out there who will aggressively pursue any potential franchise quarterback because they are so hard to find. You accept the risk. You assume the burden of making sure that Brendan Sorsby stays on the straight and narrow as it relates to gambling. You take all of that because there's a chance you're going to get a guy who's going to be your quarterback for 10 or 15 years. So, it's a hell of a reward. It's a hell of a risk, but it's a hell of a reward. I remember back in when Josh Freeman fell out of favor with Greg Shiano and eventually he was cut. Vikings signed him like that and somebody from the team explained to me at the time, look, everybody's looking for a franchise quarterback. You've got three types of teams. One team that has one. Two, team that doesn't. Three, team that has a guy on the roster that maybe becomes a franchise quarterback. We don't know yet. If you get a guy who can be put into category three and developed into category 1, that's a steal. That's what everyone's looking for. So, there will be teams that become comfortable enough to take the chance. I think there should be teams that look at this and say, "Man, it's worth," and they'll determine ahead of time what they're willing to do. It's worth a four. It's worth a three. It's worth it, too. Hard to believe anybody using next year's first round draft pick on Brendan Soresby. But you know what? If somebody at the bottom of the priority or order order decides they just love this guy, everything that they're able to glean over the course of the next five, six weeks, nothing stops them from saying we'll use our first round pick. But you're talking about a compressed time frame when the coaches and the general managers are typically off. So much for our downtime. Proday is scheduled for July 10 and there's a lot of work to be done, a lot of people to talk to, a lot of experts to consult with. You want to talk to the kid. I was on with Dan Patrick earlier today. He said, "What's one question that a team would want to ask Brendan Sorsby?" And you know, there isn't one question. It's what do we have here? What kind of a prospect is he? What do we think he can develop into in the NFL? And how recovered is he from his gambling addiction? There's been mention of an anxiety disorder, panic attacks. Does it make sense for him to be thrust into the NFL? Benefit of no offseason program. Just boom, there you are at training camp. Go sink or swim and don't gamble. And we're going to apply all of these various devices to your phone and whatnot. We're going to monitor you. like it's a challenging situation enough when you had the benefit of the offseason program and you've gotten yourself adjusted and acclimated and then you show up for training camp as a rookie. It's going to be very hard for Brendan Sorsby and you're going to have to be confident if you draft him that he's going to thrive in that environment. So, there's a lot of factors that go into it and there may not be enough time to come to the right conclusion that both physically and mentally he is good to go. And you can have some owners who say, you know, it's a great idea and maybe he turns out to be a great quarterback, but we're not comfortable giving up next year's fourth, third, second, first, whatever to try to get him. Then there's the question, and I'll choose my words carefully here. Who cares? Will the league try to tell the teams to shy away from him? Will he be black ballalled? Will the league decide in lie of, and I'm just throwing this out as a possibility, I'm not saying they're going to do it, in lie of blocking him from the supplemental draft, in lie of suspending him, we're just going to discourage anyone from drafting him. I I don't think the league would do that. It would be collusion. It would be blatant. there's a way to kind of get your message across that you're not thrilled with this guy walting into the NFL given the admitted violation of gambling laws and the violation of the NCA policies. But it's just something to keep an eye on. And I I think he should get drafted in one of the seven rounds. Does he get drafted lower at the nudging of 345 Park Avenue? I don't know. But we've seen this movie enough times to know that if the NFL wants a specific outcome, it has ways to get from point A to point B. So that's where it stands. There's a lot of work that needs to be done. There's a lot of information that needs to be gathered. There's a lot of boxes that need to be checked. And you know, when it's time to talk to Brendan Sorsby, you want full transparency. You want no hesitation. Dan made the point of medical information and privacy of that. Hey, when you come to the NFL, you know, we hear it all the time. It's a job interview. You have to open up your life to anything. Your body gets poked and prodded. You get asked a bunch of questions and do a bunch of research on you for a prospect like Sorsby who's walking into the NFL with an admitted gambling addiction he's recovering from. It raises the stakes for everyone. So, we'll be watching it. will be following it. And step one, will they let him in? Step two, would they suspend him? Step three, will he be drafted? I need to go back to the prior case and see if he was suspended after he was drafted. I vaguely recall vaguely that the suspension came after, but I could be wrong. Wouldn't be the first time I'm wrong today. All right. Next up, Rashi Rice served 30 days in jail for a probation violation. Now, the 30 days were the 30 days he had agreed to serve at some point over a 5-year period. He was going to do it a weekend at a time, a week at a time, whatever. When he had the positive marijuana test, it was over. It was done. You got to serve the 30 days right now. So, the time has been served and he's out of jail. There's video of him running away from reporters who were trying to talk to him. And in one of the items I saw last night, and I wasn't aware of this because when he was sent to jail, he had just had knee surgery and he wasn't going to be able to rehab in jail. On May 28th, the judge softened the order and allowed him to go out of the facility to get to get rehab services from May 28 on. So, he's been able to work on that knee, which is important. He's got to get himself healthy and he's going to be going forward into training camp without the benefit of the offseason program. At least the OTAAS and the mini camp. He missed all of that. I assume the Chiefs are going to find him 100,000 plus for missing the mandatory mini camp. There's no I was in jail excuse when it comes to the mandatory mini camp. And then there's the question of just what do the Chiefs really think about? Andy Reid said all the right things, but what do they really think about him? It's a contract year. It's a big year for him. He has every incentive to get all details of his life straightened out. And I know the Chiefs really, really like him. Dating back to the street racing incident. I was making some phone calls after that happened and it became obvious to me that the Chiefs have high hopes for Rashi Rice. Now remember, he had the knee injury week four of the 2024 season. Then he was suspended six games to start 2025 as a result of the street racing guilty plea. He's free and clear now to play. There's been no indication the NFL is going to take any action. We laid this out previously. They could in theory maybe try to invoke the personal conduct policy. They could in theory maybe try to use the substance abuse policy. They haven't tried to do anything. And the Chiefs has said they've got no indication that the league is going to do anything. So, he's back, but the team is shut down until training camp. He's got to keep rehabbing the knee and get himself ready to go for camp. But he needs to have a big season this year cuz they're not going to they're not going to sign him to a new contract until they are sure that these issues have been fully resolved and that he can be the player that a significant contract would justify paying that money to. Next up, and it's interesting to look at the headlines that I've seen elsewhere. The main headline as it relates to the late Alden Smith today is that his family is donating his brain for CTE research and and that's not uncommon. CTE cannot be diagnosed in a living patient. We have seen many players since the concussion crisis first went to full boil in late 2009 donate their brains to science to see whether to what extent they had CTE. Now, we still don't know what it means to live with CTE. We don't know what the various degrees of it mean. And above all else, there's no way to determine if someone has it while they're still living. But that was the headline. They they really buried the lead with that. The press release that went out from a PR firm presumably connected to the law firm that's going to be representing Smith's family. He's hired three high-profile lawyers to get to the bottom of why he's dead. And whether to what extent he had CTE as part of it, but for now, it's a mystery as to what happened to Alden Smith. He's with a friend. They delivered pizzas to a homeless shelter. They went past the friend's house. Friend goes in for a minute, comes out, and Alden Smith is unresponsive inside the friend's truck. What happened to Alden Smith? So, this is much bigger than donating his brain for CTE research. The headline is Alden Smith's family has hired lawyers to find out what happened. And in the statement, they say, "We're going to get to the bottom of it." They are confused and dismayed and obviously shocked by this turn of events. You can't have true closure until you know what happened. So, there is an effort underway with three high-profile lawyers to try to find out exactly what happened to Alden Smith. All right. Lastly for today, I saw that Calvin Johnson commented on the reality that someone's going to set the single season receiving yardage record, break his record of 1964 receiving yards from 2012. We're 5 years into this 17 game thing. I'm surprised no one's broken it yet. Someone's going to break it because it's going to 18. And I know every time someone gets close to setting a single season record in a 17 game season, there are people that want to apply an asterisk to it. The season is what it is. 12 games, 14 games, 16 games, 17 games, 18 games, 20 games. Single season record goes with the length of the season in accordians. It's still the single season record. Now, you can have subcategories. Calvin Johnson had the record in a 16game season. Someone else he thinks Pukanu has got a chance to do it. He could have the record in a 17game season. And then along comes someone who's currently still in high school who sets the record in an 18game season. So yeah, it's inevitable. It wasn't such a ridiculously dominant number. title: Sorsby applying for NFL supplemental draft still has uncertainties | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: The supplemental draft had been irrelevant for seven years. They had one in 2023. No one was picked. The last time someone was selected, 2019. There have been multiple recognizable names over the years who have entered the NFL through the supplemental draft. It has become something that is used less and less frequently in these days, but it will be a major topic in the coming days and weeks as Brendan Sorsby decides to abandon his attempt to play college football and applies for the supplemental draft. And there are a lot of questions and I've talked about some of this stuff before, but I think this is a good moment to really frame up the three big questions going forward from this point. Number one, will the NFL accept Brandon Sorsby, Brandon Sorsby, excuse me, into the supplemental draft? There's no reason for them not to. He's no longer eligible to play college football. He was eligible to play college football back in April when the regular draft happened. And the way the CBA is written, if a player becomes ineligible after the the regular draft, he can enter the supplemental draft. And he meets all the other criteria. He's at least three years out of high school. That's the one big one. So, there's nothing that should keep him out. That doesn't mean the NFL won't try to find a way to do it. The NFL's been tight lipped about this one. So, we don't know what they are thinking. The way the CBA is written, you could make the argument if you want to try to keep Brendan Sorsby out that he knew or should have known he was ineligible in advance of the most recent regular draft and he should have entered that draft. He could have. He's got the time in. He could have declared for it. He had reason to know he may not be able to play in 2026 because he's aware of his gambling habits. his gambling activities, his violation of gambling laws because he was gambling when he was under the age of 21 and his violation rampant and repeated violation of NCA bylaws. Now, that would be a very aggressive argument for the NFL to make, but that would be based on my reading of the CBA the only thing they could do if they really want to just kick this can until April of next year. They could do that. They could say, "You knew or at a minimum should have known you had lost your eligibility. It just wasn't official yet. You should have entered the regular draft in April and you decided to try to get two bites out of the apple. You decided to try to keep your eligibility, fight the NCA, and then when the walls closed in legally, you changed your mind and you bolted for the NFL. That's not me talking. That's what the NFL would say if they were to make that argument that he knew or should have known he was eligible for the regular draft and therefore he can't choose his draft. He can't pick which draft he gets selected in. Can't try to have it both ways trying to stay in college and then if all else fails, I'll go to the NFL draft. And clearly once this thing became an issue, he was trying to get clarity from the NCAA so he could make that decision. Are you going to let me play? I want to play at Texas Tech. Are you going to let me play? No. All right. I got an injunction that says you have to let me play. Problem solved. Then other lawsuits get filed. The heat got a little too hot for Texas Tech and Searsby, I think, sensitive to what Texas Tech has been going through. He pulls the plug and he has the supplemental draft. I think they should let him in. But if they want to be ultraaggressive, they could make that argument that he'd already lost his eligibility and he knew it. and it became a shell game after that for him to try to get one more year of college football, one more year of NIL money before coming to the NFL. Second question, will he be suspended by the NFL? You let him into the supplemental draft and then you impose a suspension for violation of the law, underage betting, and rampid violations of the NCA gambling rules. That one's a little trickier. I've mentioned the Terrell Prior precedent several times. He had a five-game suspension imposed on him for the 2011 season. He ended up entering the supplemental draft. The NFL imposed the same fivegame suspension, arguing that he manipulated the eligibility rules in a way that undermines the integrity of them. It wouldn't be very difficult for the NFL to come up with something, if it wants to, to make the case that betting while under the age of 21 repeatedly, betting on your team, even if you weren't playing in games, that that requires the same punishment he's escaping by leaving the NCAA. Now, it's not a perfect argument, and most legal arguments aren't. That's why there's two sides to every story. One side tries to fashion an argument rooted in relevant applicable rules language that suits their interest. The other side goes the other way. Good lawyers can come up with compelling arguments on both sides of a question. But if the NFL really wants to be not full out aggressive and keep him out of the supplemental draft, welcome him in, but suspend him. What's to stop them? He's not protected by the union until he's drafted or signs an NFL contract. So, they could, and this where this is where the the timing of a suspension becomes interesting. You suspend him before he's drafted. What standing would the union have at that point to do anything? None. Once he's drafted, the union has the ability to fight it. I don't know that the NFL will try to split the hairs that carefully. They may just wait and see if he's drafted. Now, I think he will be more on that in a second, but it could be the NFL doesn't do anything about a possible suspension until it has to, and it doesn't have to until after he's drafted. So, the Terrell Prior case from 2011 could make a suspension more likely for Sorsby. And I know that there are teams that are concerned they're going to draft this guy and he's not going to be available at all in 2026. So what's the point in giving up the draft pick early if you don't get the benefit of the player early? Another item that I believe I mentioned here and I wrote something about it today at PFT. Kan Booty very similar case gambling addiction admitted to it wrote an article for the Players Tribune earlier this year between conference championships. I believe in the Super Bowl. He was drafted by the Patriots in 2023. After his rookie season, it came to light that he was being arrested for underage gambling in Louisiana. Made at least six bets on LSU while he was on the LSU team. The charges were later dropped and the NFL did nothing. Nothing. Now, the big difference is he was already in the NFL for a season. And from a PR standpoint, and so much of this stuff really is PR, the decisions the NFL makes from a disciplinary standpoint, the personal conduct policy in and of itself is a PR tool. It's not a judicial tool. It's a quasi judicial device to enhance and promote and support the NFL's PR efforts. But if you act against Booty after he's been in the NFL for a full season, you draw attention to the fact that you had no idea. What kind of vetting are you guys doing when you have no idea that this guy who you have welcomed into the draft class was rampantly and repeatedly gambling? So, I could see why the NFL decides not to do anything with Booty because he's already in the NFL. But with Sorsby, it's front and center. It's a big deal. In the aftermath of last week's court ruling, it was one of the biggest stories in sports. So even though what they didn't do with Kahan Booty would seem to apply and would seem to suggest they shouldn't do anything with Brendan Sorsby, the difference is they know about Sorsby before he ever plays. And we we know we know how the NFL operates. This isn't criticism. It's reality. They do whatever they want to do case by case. They don't like to be bound by precedent. They don't like to have third parties making decisions based on past practices and fairness, etc. They just want to do what they think is right in this case. What is right for us right now? Right now, this is a big deal. A lot of questions about integrity of sport and big headlines and a lot of discussion and let's just take some of the steam out of this. Also, as I've said before, they may want to plate the NCA. If the NCA doesn't want this guy to play in 2026, if they view it as a punishment, he shouldn't be allowed to play in 2026. If that's conveyed directly or indirectly, overtly or subtly to the NFL, they may feel compelled to to act accordingly. The last bit of precedent, and this is from a question that a reader asked. I had forgotten about this. When Jim Harbaugh left Michigan for his return to the NFL, at one point Ian Raport of NFL Media, which at the time was owned and operated by the league, said basically if Harbaugh comes back, he's going to get suspended because he's subject to suspension by the NCAA. Well, that never happened. There was never anything. There was never even a serious conversation publicly about the possibility of Harbaugh suffering any consequences for the various things that went on when he was at Michigan. So if I'm arguing on behalf of Brendan Sorsby, I'm pointing to Harbaugh and I'm pointing to Kahan Booty and I'm pointing out that what they did to Terrell Prior in 15 years ago shouldn't have happened. And as we reported last night, Jeffrey Kesler already putting the NFL on notice. I'm told that he's going to make sure that they don't try to either not accept him into the supplemental draft or suspend him once he gets there. Now, the bigger question is this, and this relates to what happens if he's allowed into the supplemental draft and it's time for the teams to start figuring out what they're going to do. And the procedure, I found this in an SI article from about the time this all first came up. They split the league into three categories. Teams with six or fewer wins or fewer than six wins, teams with six or more wins that didn't make the playoffs, and then all the teams that made the playoffs. So, you have three buckets of teams. They do a weighted lottery. So, there really is an NFL draft lottery. We just didn't we didn't really know about it. They haven't monetized it yet. It's not a tentpole event yet, the supplemental draft lottery, but they do a lottery to determine who's got priority among those three buckets. And then each round the team decides ahead of time, am I basically going to bid? It's like a silent auction. I'm going to bid this pick and you bid it for let's say round three, well, if you have priority as opposed to the other teams that made the bid, you get him. That's a dynamic that could get someone who maybe made the playoffs last year or got close to it think better go around earlier if I want this guy. So if the consensus is he's round three, you may have to go round two to get him. if you're going to be low in the priority list, but everybody will know what their priority is. So, that's part of the the guessing game that a team is going to need to make. Do I pull the trigger this round or do I wait until next round because next round somebody higher in the pecking order may get him before we can. Hi, it's Mike Fuio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. Hit subscribe for the latest news and analysis from Pro Football

title: Can Rashee Rice follow through on Kansas City Chiefs' high hopes? | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: Rashee Rice served 30 days in jail for a probation violation. Now, the 30 days were the 30 days he had agreed to serve at some point over a 5-year period. He was going to do it a weekend at a time, a week at a time, whatever. When he had the positive marijuana test, it was over, it was done. He had to serve the 30 days right now. So, the time has been served and he's out of jail. There's video of him running away from reporters who were trying to talk to him. And in one of the items I saw last night, and I wasn't aware of this, because when he was sent to jail, he had just had knee surgery and he wasn't going to be able to rehab in jail. On May 28th, the judge softened the order and allowed him to go out of the facility to get to get rehab services from May 28th on. So, he's been able to work on that knee, which is important. He's got to get himself healthy. And he's going to be going forward into training camp without the benefit of the off-season program, at least the OTAs and the mini camp. He missed all of that. I assume the Chiefs are going to fine him 100,000 plus for missing the mandatory mini camp. There's no I was in jail excuse when it comes to the mandatory mini camp. And then there's the question of just what do the Chiefs really think about him? Andy Reid said all the right things, but what do they really think about him? It's a contract year, it's a big year for him. He has every incentive to get all details of his life straightened out. And I know the Chiefs really, really like him. Dating back to the street racing incident, I was making some phone calls after that happened and it became obvious to me that the Chiefs have high hopes for Rashee Rice. Now, remember he had the knee injury week four of the 2024 season, then he was suspended six games to start 2025 as a result of the street racing guilty plea. He's free and clear now to play. There's been no indication the NFL is going to take any action. We laid this out previously. They could, in theory, maybe try to invoke the personal conduct policy. They could, in theory, maybe try to use the substance abuse policy. They haven't tried to do anything, and the Chiefs have said they've got no indication that the league is going to do anything. So, he's back, but the team is shut down until training camp. He's got to keep rehabbing the knee and get himself ready to go for camp, and he needs to have a big season this year. Cuz they're not going to They're not going to sign him to a new contract until they are sure that these issues have been fully resolved and that he can be the player that a significant contract would justify paying that money to. Hi, it's Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. Hit subscribe for the latest news and analysis from Pro Football Talk.

title: Will NFL teams shy away from Brendan Sorsby? | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: the separate question and this is again crystallized by all of the criticism, all the discussion, the hand ringing, everything that happened after the ruling was issued last Monday. Will there be teams that shy away from Brendan Sorsby? You got 32 teams now. 31 can say no. All it takes is one to say yes. I don't think it's ludicrous to think there are some teams and specifically their owners. When you're talking about significant draft capital, the owner is going to be involved. When you're talking about getting a quarterback who could be groomed to become your future starter, the owner is going to be involved. And if the owner isn't comfortable with what is known or knowable between now and the time the supplemental draft comes, if you're not comfortable, you're not going to greenlight it. Quarterback touches the ball every single play. We don't need to have on our team the risk of a quarterback who has a gambling addiction that he's trying to recover from having a relapse. We don't want to spend our time policing him hard enough to run a football team without having to constantly monitor one of the players who has a gambling addiction in a sport that is fueled by gambling where the owners are allowed to own up to 5% of a company that runs a sports book. where the NFL has traditionally, not yet, but they eventually will, had lucrative sponsorships with sports books, where you see the ads everywhere. We're not comfortable taking that chance. That's going to be the balance. And there will be some owners who are conservative, small C conservative, who are careful, and they just don't want to they don't want to run that risk. You got to weigh the talent against the risk. And that becomes part of this analysis as well. How good do we think he'll be based upon his time primarily at Cincinnati? Will he be potentially a consistent, viable starting quarterback? Could he become a Pro Bowler? Could he become a franchise quarterback? And you know, there are teams out there who will aggressively pursue any potential franchise quarterback because they are so hard to find. You accept the risk. You assume the burden of making sure that Brendan Sorsby stays on the straight and narrow as it relates to gambling. You take all of that because there's a chance you're going to get a guy who's going to be your quarterback for 10 or 15 years. So, it's a hell of a reward. It's a hell of a risk, but it's a hell of a reward. I remember back in when Josh Freeman fell out of favor with Greg Shiano and eventually he was cut. Vikings signed him like that and somebody from the team explained to me at the time, look, everybody's looking for a franchise quarterback. You've got three types of teams. One team that has one. Two, team that doesn't. Three, team that has a guy on the roster that maybe becomes a franchise quarterback. We don't know yet. If you get a guy who can be put into category three and developed into category 1, that's a steal. That's what everyone's looking for. So, there will be teams that become comfortable enough to take the chance. I think there should be teams that look at this and say, "Man, it's worth," and they'll determine ahead of time what they're willing to do. It's worth a four. It's worth a three. It's worth it, too. Hard to believe anybody using next year's first round draft pick on Brendan Soresby. But you know what? If somebody at the bottom of the priority or order order decides they just love this guy, everything that they're able to glean over the course of the next five, six weeks, nothing stops them from saying we'll use our first round pick. But you're talking about a compressed time frame when the coaches and the general managers are typically off. So much for our downtime. Proday is scheduled for July 10 and there's a lot of work to be done, a lot of people to talk to, a lot of experts to consult with. You want to talk to the kid. I was on with Dan Patrick earlier today. He said, "What's one question that a team would want to ask Brendan Sorsby?" And you know, there isn't one question. It's what do we have here? What kind of a prospect is he? What do we think he can develop into in the NFL? And how recovered is he from his gambling addiction? There's been mention of an anxiety disorder, panic attacks. Does it make sense for him to be thrust into the NFL? Benefit of no offseason program. Just boom, there you are at training camp. Go sink or swim and don't gamble. And we're going to apply all of these various devices to your phone and whatnot. We're going to monitor you. like it's a challenging situation enough when you had the benefit of the offseason program and you've gotten yourself adjusted and acclimated and then you show up for training camp as a rookie. It's going to be very hard for Brendan Sorsby and you're going to have to be confident if you draft him that he's going to thrive in that environment. So, there's a lot of factors that go into it and there may not be enough time to come to the right conclusion that both physically and mentally he is good to go. And you can have some owners who say, you know, it's a great idea and maybe he turns out to be a great quarterback, but we're not comfortable giving up next year's fourth, third, second, first, whatever to try to get him. Then there's the question, and I'll choose my words carefully here. Who cares? Will the league try to tell the teams to shy away from him? Will he be black ballalled? Will the league decide in lie of, and I'm just throwing this out as a possibility, I'm not saying they're going to do it. In lie of blocking him from the supplemental draft, in lie of suspending him, we're just going to discourage anyone from drafting him. I I don't think the league would do that. It would be collusion. It would be blatant. there's a way to kind of get your message across that you're not thrilled with this guy walting into the NFL given the admitted violation of gambling laws and the violation of the NCAA policies. But it's just something to keep an eye on. And I I think he should get drafted in one of the seven rounds. Does he get drafted lower at the nudging of 345 Park Avenue? I don't know. But we've seen this movie enough times to know that if the NFL wants a specific outcome, it has ways to get from point A to point B. So that's where it stands. There's a lot of work that needs to be done. There's a lot of information that needs to be gathered. There's a lot of boxes that need to be checked. And you know, when it's time to talk to Brendan Sorsby, you want full transparency. You want no hesitation. Dan made the point of medical information and privacy of that. Hey, when you come to the NFL, you know, we hear it all the time. It's a job interview. You have to open up your life to anything. Your body gets poked and prodded. You get asked a bunch of questions and do a bunch of research on you for a prospect like Sorsby who's walking into the NFL with an admitted gambling addiction he's recovering from. It raises the stakes for everyone. So, we'll be watching it. will be following it. And step one, will they let him in? Step two, would they suspend him? Step three, will he be drafted? title: ESPN’s Josh Pate Talks Brendan Sorsby & Texas Tech Controversy with Rich Eisen | Full Interview
text: Josh Pate of the Josh Pate College Football Show and all the other spots on ESPN right here on the Rich Eisen Show. All right, Josh, what happened in Texas Tech over the last 8 days after we last talked with Brendan Sorsby getting a ruling in his favor to play this year? >> Well, I think maybe some people calculated that eventually, if they turned the eye of the stove off, it would just slowly cool down, it would slowly diffuse, and really when they got that injunction, maybe people thought it would go that way. It did not go that way. As it turned out, it was never going to go that way. And a couple of things that were key indicators to me, Rich, were number one, when they got the injunction, which led to a high likelihood he was going to play. Not a certainty, but a high likelihood he was going to play. I thought Texas Tech needed to just keep their mouths shut. I thought the best, most shrewd PR move at that point would be to tell them, "Shut up. Don't say a word. You just got a favorable ruling. Vast majority of the college football public and just society at large looks at it and thinks that's the wrong decision. They think it's more a loophole or a breakdown in the structure than something that should have happened. Nothing you say at this point is going to turn an ounce of public opinion your way." Well, they released a 22-minute video with five guys from Texas Tech, all some of whom I know very, very closely. They're great people. They were largely telling the truth in that video, but it didn't matter because of the optics of it. No one even bothered to listen to the video. They just saw it as, "Oh, well, they got their way, and now they're going to try and gaslight us into explaining why this is a good thing, or they're trying to explain their The public didn't have time for it. The public didn't want to hear it. That was part one that led me to realize this is not going anywhere." But then part two, I don't pretend to understand all the legal-ese of this, but the Texas Attorney General, Ken Paxton, when he sent that letter sort of on behalf of Texas Tech the other day, as it's been explained to me, that opened a whole new door. That opened a whole new can of worms on this thing, and it provided the Big 12 and the other member institutions in the Big 12 who were not prepared to take this lying down. It provided them legal recourse. It it allowed them to return the serve, in other words. And I think even over the last 24 hours, it became very apparent the dam had broken and it became very apparent we're fighting a losing battle. At this point, uh the temperature has changed, the wind direction has changed, and then it's just I don't know if they feel this way, but I feel in the immediate aftermath of him declaring for the supplemental draft, it's best for all parties. Cuz you can never prove a counterfactual, like you can never know how something was going to play out when it doesn't. But I don't think it takes too creative a mind, Rich, to go down the road of what it would have been like at Big 12 media days. What it would have been like in the lead-up to week one. What it would have been like maybe with you know, people with political aspirations in other Big 12 states trying to make a name for themselves the week that they're going to play Texas Tech and trying to get injunctions and trying to do all this sort of thing. It was going to be a really really ugly scene for everyone involved. And so now you rid yourself of that, and look for it for the Texas Tech piece of all this, I think there were a lot of lessons learned out there. Cuz in moments of crisis, like you're if you're a major organization, you want a united voice. You want a single voice. And it felt like there were about three or four different voices coming out of Lubbock. And it's just as long as you learn from it, it's not a total failure. And I could say that about Brendan Soursby. I could say that about the NCAA. I could say that about a lot of entities here. But I think the end result here is, yeah, things changed, and the result of those things changing, I think, is a net win for all parties involved. >> Well, it's not just that, too, Josh. It's this 22-year-old quarterbacks in college football are supposed to be enjoying the spotlight or trying to with the spotlight they're trying to deal with is the pressure of of playing the position. Um not being the avatar of what's wrong in college athletics, which is what Brendan Sorsby has been for quite some time. And even if you do feel, for whatever reason, that his um his checking into uh an inpatient rehab program was part of the plan to try and get a judge to say, "This is an affliction that the NCAA should be trying to help him through, not punish him for what caused him to go in." Um that you're still talking about a 22-year-old kid with clearly something in his on his brain, on his mind, that needs to be dealt with. Do any any Anybody know how he's doing right now through all of this, Josh? Or that's just kind of second, third hand information that nobody's really checking in on, you know? >> Uh to my knowledge, he hasn't spoken publicly. >> Right. >> I haven't talked to him. Uh he was he wasn't in the building, to my knowledge, when I was out there a couple of weeks ago. >> So, I mean, it's a it's it's actually interesting that you asked that question, which means it's a good question. I don't know. I have no idea. >> I will say this, um maybe this will be spoken about a little bit more in the coming weeks when there's nothing left to lose and people unpack their real feelings on this. You know, it was viewed externally as Texas Tech was making every move here. You know, Texas Tech was the one making every argument. And to some degree, they did. Brendan Sorsby and his camp, if you want to call it that, they were sort of the ones leading charge on this. They were the ones leading the charge on, you know, filing this, filing that, saying this, saying that. Now, ultimately, it doesn't really matter. It's the same message. Where it's coming from is sort of irrelevant. The only reason I present that is the question you just asked. Whether he's going to be eligible this year or not or whether he's going to play college football this year or not. Well, if if the basis for the reason for this whole thing is to be believed, and I believe it, well, then that reality's still there. If you're talking to me about gambling addiction as the reason for all this, well, that reason's still there. And I've never suffered from addiction personally. Many of us have. Many people in this audience have. There may be people in the audience that have suffered and are currently dealing with gambling addiction. But whatever kind of addiction it is, there's not an off switch on it. And so if it is to be believed that this was authentic, and I got every reason to believe it was, well, that's something that's ongoing. And until we hear from him, and until we get full testimonial from that side of the table, so to speak, that answer is anyone's guess. >> And then one of the posts that I saw across my screen today is like a clip from Planes, Trains, and Automobiles of John Candy with Steve Martin after they have a uh scary, life-changing experience, and Steve Martin is just absolutely done with John Candy, just livid with him. And John Candy's laughing and saying, "Wow, we can laugh about it now that we're we're all right, right?" And John Candy has the Texas Tech logo on him. Steve Martin has the Big 12 logo on him. And it was brilliant. It's funny, but also somewhat true. Like, what's the relation Like, what what happens now that this thing has gone in this direction? Josh. >> I don't know that that thing thaws for a while. And it's just just kind of me feeling it from the outside. There were some things said. There were some shots taken. I Rich, I fully believe there was a movement mounting to take matters into their own hands as a conference because what do we have? I don't even know, 15 or 16 teams in that league. Well, whatever that number is minus one, the one being Texas Tech, everyone else was in pretty much lockstep that this is the wrong move, that we don't want him playing there, we don't think he should be able to play there. Whatever [snorts] you feel about that's whatever you feel about that and Texas Tech's well aware of that. And Texas Tech, mind you, this is already a program This is already a group of people, Lubbock, Texas, culturally West Texas, the vibe is already defaulted to it's sort of an us against the world mentality out here. West Texas is a long way from Dallas and Houston. It is a different planet than those places. I happen to love it out there. Most of America's never been there. And so when you combine that attitude and the defensive nature, the willingness to fight at a moment's notice, when you combine that with the circumstances that just presented themselves, maybe it contextualizes Texas Tech's actions a little bit more in this, but then like you said, once it's kind of gone, the lingering effect is Texas Tech feeling some type of way towards their own conference. No one's forgetting this, you know, it's situation's done, no one's forgetting it. So I think it may be frosty for quite a while. >> And the Sourcesby camp didn't see a lot of this coming or didn't think about it or you know what I mean? Like hey, if we force if we do get this ruling, there will be such holy heck going on that it might not even be worth the squeeze to the point where you may have to go to the NFL cuz we're not going to get a resolution prior to that safety valve having a June 22nd deadline, right? Like they didn't see that coming? You don't >> I really think there was a lot of underestimation about how much blowback there would be because of the specifics of this. You know, you could you could take this into another compartment. Maybe a guy's got a an ongoing investigation into some type of criminal behavior activity or whatever and that may be in the societal scope of things way worse than betting on games but strictly within the confines of the sport the outcomes of the games and the integrity of it that's paramount and that was you know what had everyone up in arms the NCAA I mean they they stumbled nine ways from Sunday when it come to the came to the Baylor situation the sexual assault situation a long time ago but like a lot of people look at the NCAA and don't even expect them to be capable of being the governing body that oversees investigating that or maybe the Penn State deal before the Baylor deal but enforcing basic rules like you can't bet on the games well that should be inside the NCAA's purview and so I think they looked at it Rich and I think they severely underestimated the blowback if they did get their injunction on that they thought they could game the system here and they thought because of the way the calendar works if we get our injunction we can just drag it out and we'll play our season and at that point it'll be moot and look maybe if the circumstances didn't involve betting maybe people would begrudgingly look at it and say oh well system's broken they were just it was a pill that no one was willing to swallow on this and that's why it is really important those crisis management teams those PR firms they get paid a lot of money in these cases you've got to have someone that can see through the fog and guide you on this stuff otherwise you you act in a nature that really makes it look like you're unaware of how the outside world is thinking >> and interestingly enough Josh just to put a a ribbon on it I mean you do think that that should be within the purview of the NCAA to have teeth in handling some sort of a gambling suspension. Yet, what really did start this is what you said. What really got the ball rolling was the Big 12 saying, "We feel we should suspend him under our rules." And Ken Paxton, the the Attorney General of Texas, basically filing preemptively saying, "If you try that, there's going to be a big hell to pay." And then other attorneys general in other states in the Big 12 are like, "Well, we're going to chime in, too." And that seemed to raise this a heck of a lot more than the NCAA saying, "We want a an expedited answer on whether this ruling that Sources got two Mondays ago can get handled now." It seems like the Big 12 and the attorneys generals or attorneys general getting involved, that was it. That seemed to be the one that it was the accelerant. >> A lot of people who I view as being far or smarter and more adept legally than me have said point-blank, "If Ken Paxton doesn't say what he said, if he doesn't write that letter, Brendan Sorsby's probably playing for Texas Tech this fall. So, whatever that domino was, that's a really, really big domino because legally what it did, and again, I'm going to skate around this cuz I'm not going to try and use terms I don't understand, it provided the Big 12 the ability to do something legally more than just yell and shout and and put out statements on Twitter. Once that happened, and once he used the language that he did, it was game on." >> Josh, thanks for the time. Greatly appreciate it. Well, I look forward to chatting with you more, brother. Thanks again. Hey, you made it all the way to the end. Thanks for that. Check us out every single day streaming live on Disney Plus and the ESPN app 12 to 3 Eastern.
